item.title: Early neurocognitive outcomes following SEEG with radiofrequency thermocoagulation.
item.description:
Epilepsia open
Objective Characterization of early neuropsychological outcomes following SEEG with radiofrequency thermocoagulation (RFTHC) is essential to guide patient expectations around return to work, study, and caregiving. The current study aimed to describe the early neurocognitive sequelae of SEEG. Methods Consecutive patients undergoing SEEG were prospectively recruited from two tertiary epilepsy centers in Melbourne, Australia. Patients were administered the Repeatable Battery for the Assessment of Neuropsychological Status (RBANS) via telehealth before and 3 weeks after SEEG (M = 19.69 days, SD = 4.41). Given the telehealth platform, the coding subtest was substituted for the Symbol Digit Modalities Test, and a modified score of global cognitive function was calculated. To evaluate group changes, paired sample t-tests were performed. Reliable change indices were computed to explore individual-level changes. Pearson's correlation coefficients evaluated relationships between change in global cognitive function and SEEG admission variables. SEEG patients were invited to complete a semi-structured interview canvassing the recovery following SEEG. Results Twenty-eight patients completed the neuropsychological examination (M = 37.89 years, SD = 9.72, range = 17-56 years, 54% female). All patients underwent RFTHC with a mean of 11.43 (SD = 6.87, range = 2-28) coagulation sites. At a whole group level, 3-weeks post SEEG there was no evidence for global nor domain-specific cognitive change. Reliable change indices with 90% confidence revealed only 4% (1/28) declined on at least two measures and 10% (3/28) showed psychometric improvement. Pearson's correlational coefficients showed no evidence for association between change in global cognitive function with SEEG factors including admission length, number of spontaneous or stimulated seizures, number of electrodes, or number of RFTHC sites. Subjective reports of language change tended to be accompanied by a decline on the RBANS language index that did not meet reliable change criteria. Most patients reported returning to work around 4 weeks post SEEG. Significance By 3 weeks, gross cognitive functioning tends to be in keeping with pre-SEEG performances for most patients. These findings have direct clinical implications for SEEG neuropsychological counseling. Plain language statement SEEG is increasingly used to guide epilepsy surgery. Despite this, little is known about the cognitive recovery in the weeks following the procedure. We found that for most patients, broad cognitive functioning 3 weeks after SEEG with coagulation was consistent with function before SEEG, with only a small minority showing significant changes. Some people who reported language difficulties also showed a decline on language testing, although this was often small. Of those patients working before SEEG, most returned to work by 4 weeks. These results provide important evidence to guide patient counseling, recovery planning, and management after SEEG.

item.title: Validation of the diagnosis of Lennox-Gastaut syndrome: Challenges and lessons learned.
item.description:
Epilepsia
Objective Lennox-Gastaut Syndrome (LGS) is a severe developmental and epileptic encephalopathy characterized by multiple seizure types, cognitive impairment, and distinct electroencephalographic (EEG) findings. However, evolving diagnostic criteria, heterogeneous clinical features, and inconsistent electronic health record (EHR) documentation complicate accurate diagnosis and cohort identification. As part of a Patient-Centered Outcomes Research Institute-sponsored study developing EHR-based computable phenotypes for LGS, we established a reference standard through retrospective chart review and epileptologist classification. Methods A multicenter retrospective chart review was conducted across seven pediatric epilepsy centers. Stratified sampling using PCORnet data selected patients based on the International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision diagnosis code for LGS or other intractable epilepsy diagnoses between 2016 and 2022. Clinical teams abstracted seizure history, EEG findings, developmental status, and treatment history. Two epileptologists independently reviewed each case as classic LGS, pragmatic LGS, or not LGS. Discordant cases underwent adjudication by a senior epileptologist. Cases with incomplete or unclear data underwent repeat abstraction and review. Results Of 997 identified patients, 935 underwent classification after exclusions. Initial epileptologist disagreement occurred in 105 cases (11%, unweighted Cohen kappa = 82%). Following adjudication, 130 cases underwent reabstraction to retrieve additional EEG reports and clinical details. Rereview reclassified 67 cases initially considered "not LGS": 33 classic LGS, 12 pragmatic LGS, and 22 excluded for insufficient data. Key EHR challenges included inconsistent EEG reporting, incomplete seizure type characterization, fragmented documentation of cognitive impairment, unclear age at onset, and variable terminology across institutions and providers. Slow spike-and-wave EEG findings were the most frequently missing diagnostic element. Significance Validating LGS diagnoses using EHR data is complex and resource intensive. Standardized terminology, structured documentation, and rigorous multicenter validation may improve diagnostic accuracy, research cohort identification, computable phenotype development, and longitudinal care for individuals with LGS. Our results highlight important operational lessons for multicenter rare epilepsy studies and underscore the need for improved diagnosis pathways and longitudinal care systems for those with LGS and their families.

item.title: Symptom-related damage patterns in mesial temporal lobe epilepsy with hippocampal sclerosis.
item.description:
Epilepsia
Objective This study was undertaken to elucidate the neuroanatomical and network substrates underlying diverse seizure symptoms in mesial temporal lobe epilepsy with hippocampal sclerosis (mTLE-HS) by applying multivariate support vector regression (SVR) to individualized structural symptom mapping and atrophy network mapping (ANM). Methods We retrospectively enrolled 216 patients with mTLE-HS and 460 healthy controls. Six non-mutually exclusive seizure symptoms were assessed. We performed left-right flipping of all images of right-sided mTLE-HS patients along the midline before processing the data. Individual atrophy gray matter maps were derived using normative modeling. Structural symptom mapping was performed using multivariate SVR lesion-symptom mapping. For each patient, indirect ANM maps were generated using a normative functional connectome and direct ANM maps using the patient's own resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging. Correspondence between the two ANM approaches was assessed using individual-level whole-brain spatial correlations of unthresholded maps and group-level Dice coefficients of thresholded maps. Results Individual structural atrophy patterns were spatially heterogeneous, whereas different seizure manifestations were associated with partially distinct structural patterns and more spatially convergent network-level associations. Focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures were associated with thalamic network involvement, gestural/limb automatisms with anterior cingulate-related networks, ictal vocalization symptoms with perisylvian language networks, dysmnesia with hippocampal-posteromedial networks, emotional phenomena with prefrontal-temporal networks, and autonomic phenomena with medial prefrontal and limbic networks. Furthermore, limited spatial correspondence was observed between the results of the direct and indirect atrophy network analyses, suggesting the indirect and direct ANM can be regarded as nonequivalent but potentially complementary approaches. Significance In mTLE-HS, heterogeneous seizure manifestations are associated with distinct patterns of atrophy and distributed functional network involvement. ANM provides a complementary framework for characterizing symptom-related network patterns, and differences between indirect/normative and direct/patient-specific connectome analyses may provide complementary information.

item.title: Epilepsy as an Initial Presentation of Superficial Siderosis of the Central Nervous System:A Case Report
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Background Superficial siderosis of the central nervous system (SSCNS) is a rare neurological disorder resulting from chronic subarachnoid haemorrhage. Its classical clinical features comprise sensorineural hearing loss, cerebellar ataxia and pyramidal tract dysfunction. However, epilepsy as an initial presentation remains uncommon and insufficiently characterized. Case Presentation: We describe a 34-year-old male with a remote history of right brachial plexus injury, who presented with recurrent epileptic seizures as the predominant early symptom, followed by progressive hearing loss and gait instability. Neuroimaging demonstrated characteristic haemosiderin deposition on T2*-weighted and susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI) sequences.Transient, seizure-related subcortical and periventricular restricted diffusion on diffusion-weighted imaging resolved completely within one month. Anti-epileptic medication achieved partial seizure control, but the patient’s neurological deficits exhibited gradual progression. Conclusion Epilepsy may represent an uncommon initial presentation of SSCNS. Targeted MRI sequences facilitate diagnosis. SSCNS should be considered in the differential diagnosis of patients with unexplained epilepsy,particularly those with a history of craniospinal trauma.

item.title: Slow-wave sleep selectively amplifies network signatures of the presumed epileptogenic zone in focal epilepsy.
item.description:
Sleep
Study objectives Slow-wave sleep increases interictal epileptiform discharges (IEDs) and seizures in focal epilepsy, but how sleep stages reshape epileptogenic tissue remains unclear. We assessed whether sleep stages selectively modulate network properties of the presumed epileptogenic zone (pEZ) relative to irritative (IZ) and non-involved (NIZ) zones. Methods We studied 22 patients with drug-resistant focal epilepsy undergoing pre-surgical intracranial electroencephalography (iEEG). IED-free resting-state epochs spanned four vigilance stages: wakefulness, non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep stages 2 and 3, and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep. Spectral power, functional connectivity, graph-theoretic indices, and the 1/f exponent were quantified across seven frequency bands. Sleep stage and zone interactions were tested using permutation testing. pEZ electrodes were classified using elastic net logistic regression with leave-one-subject-out cross-validation. Results NREM3 selectively amplified within-pEZ gamma-band synchrony beyond surrounding zones (pEZ-NIZ: d=1.204, P=0.027). pEZ local efficiency and betweenness centrality rose in beta1 and gamma bands versus wakefulness. The aperiodic exponent steepened within the IZ versus NIZ during NREM3 and NREM2 (d =1.452 and 0.87, P < 0.001 and P=0.015). A three-feature classifier (NREM3 aperiodic exponent, beta2 connectivity, gamma local efficiency) localised the pEZ without ictal recordings (median AUC 0.859 pEZ vs. non-pEZ). Conclusions Slow-wave sleep selectively unmasks pEZ network properties via amplified power, synchrony and hub topology. NREM3-derived multimodal features may complement conventional pre-surgical biomarkers. Prospective validation in larger cohorts is needed to determine whether these markers improve surgical planning and outcome prediction.

item.title: Investigating fatigability and cortical activation during prolonged foot tapping in multiple sclerosis.
item.description:
Neuroscience
People with multiple sclerosis (pwMS) often exhibit motor fatigability and reduced foot-tapping ability. However, the coupling between performance and cortical activity during fast, repetitive and prolonged ankle movements remains unexplored. We aimed to investigate the neural correlates of a prolonged foot-tap task (FTT) in pwMS and healthy controls (HC). Thirty-nine pwMS (EDSS 4[3.5], 55[14] years) and 18 HC (54.5[9.75) years) performed one 1-minute FTT for each foot. Wearable sensors and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) quantified motor performance and cortical activity, respectively. fNIRS covered bilaterally frontopolar, dorsolateral prefrontal, primary motor (M1) and supplementary motor area cortices. Data were segmented into 10-second intervals and analysed via two-way ANOVA (group × time). Spearman's correlations evaluated associations between changes in cortical activity and performance (6th vs 1st segment). PwMS showed worse FTT performance with lower DLPFC activation compared to HC. On the other hand, comparable FTT performance decline over time were observed in both pwMS and HC. Cortical activity increased in SMA in HC (6 vs 2-3 intervals), but not in pwMS. In HC's, increased cortical activity across all cortical regions in the 6th interval was positive and moderately associated with less worsening in tapping performance. On the other hand, increased M1 activity was weakly associated with less foot tapping in pwMS. PwMS exhibited reduced foot-tap performance, accompanied by reduced DLPFC activation. While increased cortical activity leads to better performance in HC (i.e., a neural compensatory strategy), in pwMS increased activity was associated with worse performance (i.e., neural inefficiency).

item.title: Altered resting-state EEG microstate dynamics are associated with auditory hallucinations in patients with major depressive disorder.
item.description:
Journal of affective disorders
Background Auditory hallucination experiences are an understudied but clinically significant feature of major depressive disorder (MDD). Although EEG microstate abnormalities have been reported in MDD, their relationship with auditory hallucination experiences remains unclear. This study investigated resting-state EEG microstate dynamics associated with auditory hallucination experiences in first-episode MDD. Methods A total of 182 first-episode patients with MDD and 95 healthy controls underwent resting-state EEG recordings. Patients were classified according to lifetime history of auditory hallucination experiences into those with (AH+, n = 42) and without (AH-, n = 140) such experiences. Patients were either psychotropic medication-naïve or minimally medicated (<2 weeks of cumulative exposure). Microstate parameters were compared among groups. ANCOVA and hierarchical binary logistic regression were performed to examine associations with auditory hallucination experiences. Results Only microstate C occurrence was significantly higher in the AH+ group than in both the AH- and healthy control groups after multiple-comparison correction. This difference remained significant after adjustment for age, sex, education, and depression severity. Hierarchical logistic regression showed that higher microstate C occurrence was independently associated with auditory hallucination experiences (OR = 1.773, 95% CI: 1.211-2.595, p = 0.003), but not with hallucination severity. Its discriminatory ability was modest (AUC = 0.614, 95% CI: 0.516-0.711). Conclusions In first-episode MDD, a lifetime history of auditory hallucination experiences was associated with increased microstate C occurrence. This finding suggests that altered microstate C dynamics may represent an electrophysiological correlate of auditory hallucination experiences, warranting further investigation.

item.title: A Chronnectogram-ICA Framework for Tracking Continuously Evolving and Overlapping Functional Brain States
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
The discrete-state model of brain dynamics has become the dominant paradigm in functional connectivity analysis, representing network activity as transitions among a fixed set of transiently recurring states while generally assuming that the states themselves do not evolve. We introduce a multilevel chronnectogram framework that relaxes this assumption and explicitly represents the higher-order temporal structure of brain dynamics, how distinct states couple and co-evolve over time, alongside the persistence of each state. The method integrates spatially guided independent component analysis (ICA) with subject-specific, state-guided dynamic ICA to capture evolving and overlapping connectivity patterns in a shared representational space. Validation on simulations with known ground truth shows recovery of continuous overlap and higher-order coupling structure invisible to discrete-state methods. Applied to resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging from the FBIRN dataset (151 schizophrenia, 160 controls), the framework reveals that the same pair of brain states is shifted toward opposite extremes across patients, with strong synchrony in some and active anti-coupling in others, creating a redistribution of connectivity regimes invisible to conventional occupancy metrics, providing a substrate in which schizophrenia can appear both hyper- and hypo-volatile depending on the measure applied.

item.title: Acute stress reorganizes pregenual cingulate and subthalamic coupling to approach-avoidance decisions in remitted depression
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Major depressive disorder (MDD) is highly recurrent, and psychosocial stress is a central precipitant of relapses. Daily choices require weighing potential rewards against costs, a process disrupted in MDD that may contribute to relapse. Here, we tested whether a psychosocial stressor affects neural and computational mechanisms underlying approach-avoidance decision making in individuals with remitted MDD (rMDD, N=50) and healthy controls (N=74), prioritizing pregenual anterior cingulate cortex (pgACC) and subthalamic nucleus (STN) due to their roles in value integration and decision caution, respectively. Participants performed a dynamic approach-avoidance conflict task with fMRI before and after psychosocial stress. Hierarchical Bayesian drift-diffusion modeling evaluated whether stress modulated computational and neural mechanisms, with trial-wise pgACC and STN activity entered as neural regressors on evidence accumulation and decision threshold, respectively. Before stress, groups did not differ in any decision parameter, but pgACC activity contributed to evidence accumulation toward avoidance in controls only. After stress, rMDD showed larger increases than controls in the impact of both reward and aversiveness on accumulation toward approach and avoidance, respectively, predominantly for net-aversive offers. Furthermore, in rMDD, stress rendered both approach and avoidance decisions more sensitive to pgACC activity, and STN activity was more strongly coupled to the decision threshold than in controls. Finally, stress-induced increases in reward sensitivity in rMDD predicted one-year course of depressive symptoms. Thus, MDD remission is not characterized by a generalized blunting of decision-making, but by a latent circuit difference that acute stress reorganizes and predicts future symptoms.

item.title: Striatal tissue iron in depressed and healthy individuals and the effect of buproprion
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Introduction: Dopaminergic dysfunction in the striatum is thought to play a central role in anhedonia in major depressive disorder (MDD). Normalised T2*-weighted (nT2*w) imaging provides a widely available MRI-derived proxy of striatal tissue iron, an indirect marker of dopaminergic function, but its relationship with reward processing and anhedonia in MDD has not been established. In this secondary analysis, we examined whether striatal nT2*w distinguishes individuals with MDD from healthy controls, is associated with reward learning and clinical symptoms, including anhedonia and depression, and is sensitive to treatment with the dopaminergic antidepressant bupropion Methods Depressed (n = 40) and healthy participants (n = 41) underwent clinical assessment, functional MRI, and a probabilistic instrumental learning task (PILT) at baseline, with follow-up assessments after 2 and 6 weeks. Participants with MDD received open-label bupropion treatment throughout the 6-week study. The primary outcome was MRI-derived striatal tissue iron, quantified using nT2*w signal extracted from resting-state fMRI within the whole striatum, caudate, putamen, and nucleus accumbens. Associations between nT2*w, diagnostic group, reward learning, clinical symptoms, and treatment response were examined. Results At baseline, depressed participants compared to healthy controls showed significantly higher striatal and caudate nT2*w values, indicative of lower tissue iron. The marker demonstrated excellent 2-week test-retest reliability in healthy participants. Striatal nT2*w was not associated with reward learning, anhedonia, or depression severity at baseline, and did not change following 2 weeks of bupropion treatment or predict clinical response after 6 weeks. Across groups, females demonstrated higher nT2*w values (lower tissue iron) than males in the striatum, caudate, and putamen. Discussion Striatal nT2*w represents a promising, robust and widely accessible neuroimaging marker of depression, reliably distinguishing depressed individuals from healthy controls while demonstrating excellent test–retest reliability. Larger longitudinal studies are now needed to establish its clinical utility and determine whether it can detect changes in reward processing and treatment response across the course of illness.

item.title: Seizures Secondary to Aconitum Plant Poisoning: a case report.
item.description:
Journal of medical case reports
Background Aconitum plant poisoning typically manifests as isolated early cardiotoxicity or late neurotoxicity. However, the dynamic temporal evolution from arrhythmia-driven cardiogenic syncope to true epileptic seizures mediated by direct central nervous system injury remains rarely documented and poorly characterized. Case presentation We report a 53-year-old Han Chinese male who presented with ventricular tachycardia rapidly degenerating into ventricular fibrillation and cardiac arrest following ingestion of homemade Aconitum kusnezoffii (caowu)-infused liquor. Initial convulsions were tightly coupled with malignant arrhythmias, consistent with cardiogenic syncope. After successful resuscitation, hemoperfusion, and restoration of stable sinus rhythm, the patient developed breakthrough generalized tonic-clonic seizures on hospital days 4-6. Electroencephalography performed during sedation withdrawal revealed bilateral occipital spike-and-slow and sharp-and-slow waves with focal epileptiform discharges, confirming direct central nervous system neurotoxicity rather than recurrent cardiac ischemia. A mechanism-based, staged treatment strategy was employed: early advanced cardiac life support and hemoperfusion targeted cardiotoxicity, while sodium valproate and acetylglutamine were administered for antiepileptic prophylaxis and neuroprotection. The patient was discharged on day 13; antiepileptic therapy was successfully tapered and discontinued at 3 months without seizure recurrence, with normalization of electroencephalography and electrocardiography. Conclusions This case provides the first systematic documentation, validated by electroencephalography, of the transition from cardiogenic convulsions to true epileptic seizures in Aconitum alkaloid poisoning. The findings highlight the critical role of pharmacokinetic-driven central nervous system retention in delayed seizure onset and underscore the necessity of prolonged neurological monitoring, early electroencephalography evaluation for late-onset convulsions, and sustained antiepileptic prophylaxis to reduce mortality and long-term neurological sequelae. Key clinical message Aconitum plant poisoning may manifest as early cardiogenic syncope and convulsions secondary to malignant arrhythmias, progressing in the late stage to genuine seizures caused by central nervous system (CNS) injury. Effective management requires a staged treatment strategy targeting both cardiotoxicity and neurotoxicity, with a focus on stabilizing cardiac rhythm and providing neuroprotection as needed.

item.title: Altered glymphatic system measures and functional network connectivity in autism spectrum disorder: A longitudinal study examining associations with prognosis.
item.description:
Psychiatry and clinical neurosciences
Aim Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by social deficits and repetitive behaviors, yet prognostic biomarkers remain elusive. This study investigated the interplay between glymphatic function and functional network connectivity (FNC) in ASD and their longitudinal associations with clinical outcomes. Method This combined cross-sectional and two-year prospective longitudinal study included 50 ASD children and 50 controls. Glymphatic function was assessed using the along the perivascular space (ALPS) index and global blood-oxygen-level-dependent to cerebrospinal fluid (gBOLD-CSF) coupling, alongside FNC analysis. Results Cross-sectionally, ASD participants showed significantly reduced ALPS index, gBOLD-CSF coupling, and widespread FNC reductions. Longitudinally, among the 40 ASD participants who completed follow-up, glymphatic function increased over time. Greater increases in ALPS were correlated with greater reductions in ADOS-CSS. In the symptom-improved subgroup, four FNC connections (including DMN-DAN) increased over time. In contrast, no consistent pattern was found in the non-improved group. Baseline inter-network connectivity measures were associated with ADOS-CSS reduction in univariate analyses, but the multivariate model was not significant. Mediation analysis showed an indirect association between baseline gBOLD-CSF coupling and long-term ADOS-CSS reduction via DMN-DAN FNC reduction (indirect effect = -0.22, 95% CI [-0.42, -0.07]). Conclusion These findings indicate that glymphatic function and FNC are altered cross-sectionally and improve longitudinally in parallel with symptom changes in ASD and suggest that baseline gBOLD-CSF coupling is indirectly associated with long-term clinical improvement through DMN-DAN connectivity. Together, these results highlight the potential of glymphatic and functional connectivity measures as prognostic imaging markers in ASD.

item.title: Individualized Theta Transcranial Alternating Current Stimulation Modulates Mnemonic Discrimination and ERP Responses to Positive Information in Individuals With Elevated Depressive Symptoms.
item.description:
Social cognitive and affective neuroscience
Individuals with elevated depressive symptoms often show impairments in positive memory processing. This randomized, double-blind study investigated whether individualized theta-frequency transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) using an OFC-oriented montage modulates mnemonic discrimination and ERP responses to positive information. Sixty-one individuals with elevated depressive symptoms received either real or sham stimulation before completing an emotional mnemonic discrimination task. Behavioral results showed that lure discrimination increased following real stimulation but not sham stimulation. EEG results showed that real stimulation modulated ERP responses during positive memory encoding and retrieval, as reflected by increased late positive potential (LPP) amplitudes during encoding and altered early retrieval-related ERP amplitudes. These findings suggest that individualized theta-tACS may influence both mnemonic discrimination performance and neural responses to positive information.

item.title: Video EEG in pediatric epilepsy: Diagnostic significance and association between frequency band power and cognitive impairment severity.
item.description:
Applied neuropsychology. Child
Objective This study aimed to compare video electroencephalogram (VEEG) and routine electroencephalogram (EEG) in childhood epilepsy diagnosis and analyze the correlation between EEG frequency band power and cognitive impairment severity. Methods One hundred and sixty children suspected of having epilepsy underwent routine EEG and VEEG examinations. Diagnostic efficacy and detection rates were compared. Cognitive function was evaluated in 80 children diagnosed with epilepsy, who were allocated into normal intelligence (35 cases), borderline intelligence (25 cases), and intelligence-impaired (20 cases) groups. Clinical data, EEG parameters, and their correlation with cognitive impairment were analyzed. Results VEEG showed higher sensitivity, accuracy, and negative predictive value, and detection rates of epileptiform discharges, synchronous clinical seizures, and clinical symptoms than routine EEG (p < 0.05). Clinical characteristics and EEG parameters differed among the three groups (p < 0.05). The relative power of δ and θ bands and the awake and sleep discharge indices were positively correlated with cognitive impairment severity (r = 0.300, 0.643, 0.622, and 0.456), whereas α and β band power were negatively correlated (r = -0.515 and -0.410) (all p < 0.001). Conclusion VEEG demonstrated higher diagnostic performance than routine EEG, and EEG frequency band power was correlated with cognitive impairment severity.

item.title: Reversal of refractory epilepsy in an adult with GAMT deficiency: A case report and comparative literature review.
item.description:
Epilepsia open
Objective Guanidinoacetate methyltransferase (GAMT) deficiency is a rare autosomal recessive creatine biosynthesis disorder. Reports specifically focusing on adult patients remain scarce. Methods We report a 52-year-old female (the oldest documented case of GAMT deficiency to date) presenting with severe intellectual disability, refractory epilepsy, and adult-onset disease progression. Whole-exome sequencing identified novel compound heterozygous GAMT variants (c.265_267del and c.253G>T), and magnetic resonance spectroscopy confirmed cerebral creatine depletion. Remarkably, initiating oral creatine supplementation at age 52 achieved complete seizure freedom, normalization of the electroencephalogram (EEG), and significant motor function recovery. Results A comprehensive review revealed that untreated adult patients face a high risk of progressive neurological deterioration. Compared to the pediatric cohort, adults exhibited a significantly higher prevalence of movement disorders (69.2% vs. 33.1%, p < 0.001) and a trend toward a higher prevalence of epilepsy (92.3% vs. 74.2%). Especially, atonic seizures (drop attacks) are particularly characteristic of adult GAMT deficiency, with EEGs frequently demonstrating background slowing, multifocal epileptiform discharges, and electrodecremental patterns. Significance This study underscores that continuous disease progression and prolonged neurotoxicity still could compromise the well-being of adult GAMT deficiency patients. Accurate diagnosis is essential for adults presenting with developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE) phenotype, as even late treatment for GAMT deficiency can still dramatically alleviate the epileptic burden and reverse motor decline. Plain language summary We report the oldest known adult diagnosed with GAMT deficiency. Our case demonstrates that starting creatine treatment even at age 52 can dramatically reduce seizures and restore motor function. Literature shows that untreated adults suffer from more severe epilepsy and movement disorders than children, with symptoms worsening over time. These findings highlight the critical need for genetic testing in adults with unexplained severe epilepsy; timely creatine supplementation can halt cognitive decline and significantly restore quality of life.

item.title: Frequent involvement of cingulate and insulo-opercular regions in sleep-related hypermotor epilepsy: A multimodal presurgical study.
item.description:
Epilepsia
Objective Sleep-related hypermotor epilepsy (SHE) is classically considered a frontal lobe epilepsy; however, accumulating evidence suggests that hypermotor seizures may arise from multiple frontal and extrafrontal regions. We characterized the anatomical distribution of best available localizations in patients with SHE using multimodal presurgical data. Methods We retrospectively analyzed 17 patients with clinically diagnosed SHE who underwent comprehensive evaluation, including long-term video-electroencephalographic (EEG) monitoring, 3-T high-resolution magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography, and, where indicated, magnetoencephalography, stereo-EEG (SEEG), and surgical assessment. Best available anatomical localizations were assigned using a hierarchical multimodal framework incorporating surgical, SEEG, and concordant noninvasive findings. Their anatomical distribution was subsequently assessed at the cohort level. Results Sixteen patients (94.1%) had an assigned best available localization. Cingulate or insulo-opercular regions were involved in 11 of 16 patients (68.8%), whereas the remaining cases were localized to other frontal regions. In a sensitivity analysis restricted to 10 patients with SEEG-defined and/or surgically supported localizations, six involved cingulate or insulo-opercular regions. All patients were MRI-negative. In contrast, MRI-positron emission tomography fusion provided regionally informative anatomical findings in 16 of 17 cases and contributed to multimodal localization. Interictal epileptiform discharges were identified in 15 patients, whereas regionally informative ictal scalp EEG patterns were observed in eight; ictal interpretation was frequently limited by rapid propagation, movement-related artifacts, and delayed EEG onset. Focal cortical dysplasia-related histopathological findings were identified in five of seven resected specimens, whereas interpretation in two was limited by prior thermocoagulation. Significance These descriptive findings indicate that cingulate and insulo-opercular regions were frequently represented among the identified localizations in this presurgical cohort. Multimodal evaluation integrating electroclinical, imaging, and invasive findings may support presurgical localization in MRI-negative SHE.

item.title: Empagliflozin in Lafora disease: A first-in-human 6-month pilot study with electroclinical and FDG-PET findings.
item.description:
Epileptic disorders : international epilepsy journal with videotape
Objective Lafora disease (LD) is a rare, fatal neurodegenerative epilepsy with no approved treatments. Empagliflozin, a sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitor, has shown neuroprotective actions in preclinical models through modulation of glycogen metabolism, induction of a pseudo-ketogenic state, improved mitochondrial efficiency, and reduction of excitatory neurotransmission. Based on this rationale, we conducted a first-in-human pilot study of empagliflozin in two genetically confirmed LD patients. Methods Two patients with genetically confirmed LD received empagliflozin 10 mg/day for 6 months. Serial assessments included safety and tolerability, seizure frequency, myoclonus severity, electroencephalographic findings, neuropsychological and motor evaluations, brain MRI, and quantitative FDG-PET with regional Z-score analysis. Results Empagliflozin was safe and well tolerated, with no serious adverse events. Seizure frequency, myoclonus, and overall clinical status remained largely stable over 6 months, although some neuropsychological and motor measures showed variable changes between patients. EEG background activity and spike index were largely unchanged. Brain MRI showed stable mild cortical atrophy in both patients. In contrast, FDG-PET revealed progressive and spatially expanding cerebral hypometabolism in both patients, with worsening regional Z-scores, particularly in the parietal and precuneus regions. Significance In this first-in-human, 6-month pilot study, empagliflozin showed acceptable short-term safety and feasibility in LD, but no definitive conclusions on efficacy can be drawn. The dissociation between relative electroclinical stability and progressive metabolic impairment suggests that quantitative FDG-PET may represent a sensitive biomarker for monitoring disease trajectory in this ultra-rare epilepsy.

item.title: Altered prefrontal suppression of striatal activity during intrusive images in obsessive-compulsive disorder.
item.description:
Psychiatry and clinical neurosciences
Background Current models of obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) emphasize dysfunction in frontostriatal circuits that support flexible behavioral control, leading to impulsive and compulsive actions. However, how these disruptions contribute to obsessions and intrusive thoughts remains poorly understood. Clarifying these mechanisms is essential for understanding cognitive control deficits in OCD. Method We examined intrusive memories elicited by emotional and neutral scenes in individuals with OCD (N = 24) and healthy controls (N = 21). Participants learned scene-cue associations and were later instructed to suppress memory retrieval when presented with reminder cues. Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) measured neural activity during suppression. Generalization of findings with alternative materials was assessed in larger samples of healthy controls (N = 73) and individuals with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD; N = 55). Results fMRI analyses showed preserved activity in frontoparietal, basal ganglia, and limbic regions in individuals with OCD, even during emotional intrusion suppression. However, unlike healthy controls, individuals with OCD failed to suppress striatal activity during intrusive memory, regardless of emotional content. Connectivity analyses indicated that this hyperactivity reflected reduced top-down inhibitory control, a disruption associated with greater obsessive symptom severity. Test of generalizability confirmed the role of frontostriatal downregulation in controlling intrusive thoughts and showed that this alteration was specific to OCD. Conclusions These findings emphasize the central role of frontostriatal circuits in regulating intrusive thinking. Obsessions in OCD may result from disrupted inhibitory mechanisms that normally restrict access to striatal-dependent information, contributing to persistent intrusive thoughts.

item.title: Neuronavigated dual-target transcranial magnetic stimulation for schizophrenia negative symptoms.
item.description:
Brain : a journal of neurology
Negative symptoms in schizophrenia severely impair function and quality of life, yet respond poorly to current therapies. This multicenter, randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial aimed to investigate the efficacy of neuronavigated dual-target repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) over the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (rDLPFC) and cerebellum for improving negative symptoms in early-stage psychosis (ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT04853485). Participants with first-episode schizophrenia or clinical high-risk for psychosis were enrolled from Shanghai Mental Health Center and Suzhou Guangji Hospital. Participants were randomly assigned to either a real or sham group under MRI-guided neuronavigation, targeting rDLPFC with 1Hz at 100% motor threshold(MT), cerebellar with intermittent theta burst stimulation(iTBS) at 120% MT for 20 consecutive days. Clinical assessments were conducted at baseline(T0), 10-session(T1), 20-session(T2) and one month after the intervention(T3). Cognition and MRI were evaluated at T0 and T2. The primary outcome was change of negative subscale score of the Positive and Negative Symptoms Scale(PANSS), while secondary outcomes included alterations in other PANSS subscale scores and fronto-cerebellar circuit functional connectivity. In total, 75 participants were included in the intention-to-treat analysis (36 active, 39 sham). The pre-specified primary linear mixed-effects analysis revealed a non-significant group-by-time interaction for PANSS negative subscale scores (F(3,174.6)=1.45, p=0.230). At the 4-week endpoint (T2), the nominal unadjusted between-group p-value was 0.049; after Sidak correction for multiple comparisons, the adjusted mean difference was -2.48 points (95% CI -4.99 to 0.03, adjusted p=0.150, Cohen's d=-0.51). Descriptive uncorrected t-tests indicated greater negative-symptom reductions in the active group at T1 and T2, and the 4-week negative-symptom response rate (≥50% reduction) was higher under real rTMS (χ2=9.5, p=0.002). A significant group-by-time interaction was observed for PANSS positive subscale scores (F(3,172.0)=3.26, p=0.023). Both groups exhibited substantial within-group symptom improvement. Resting-state fMRI demonstrated group-by-time interactions within cerebello-temporal, parahippocampal, caudate, and parietal networks (FWE-corrected p<0.05), and negative-symptom change correlated with cerebello-caudate connectivity (r=0.33, p=0.026). These findings suggest neuronavigated dual-target rTMS over rDLPFC and cerebellum may be associated with numerical improvements in negative symptoms in early-stage psychosis.

item.title: Two clusters of brain regions with distinct age-related profiles of functional connectivity in autism spectrum disorder.
item.description:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
Brain functional connectivity changes throughout development, and individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) may follow trajectories that differ from those of typically developing controls. Using large multisite resting-state fMRI cross-sectional datasets, we examined how functional connectivity differences between ASD and typically developing controls change across a broad age range of 5 to 64 y. A data-driven analysis identified two spatially distributed clusters of cortical regions showing distinct age-related profiles of ASD-TD connectivity differences. Cluster 1 was marked by consistent hypoconnectivity across ages, suggesting a stable neural signature of ASD. Cluster 2 was characterized by hypoconnectivity in childhood that gradually diminished with age, suggesting a temporary delay profile. These clusters were systematically organized along the sensory-association axis. Cluster 1 mainly involved lower-rank sensory and sensorimotor cortices, while Cluster 2 mainly involved higher-rank association cortices. Brain-behavior analyses revealed greater and broader ASD symptom associations across ages in the consistent hypoconnectivity profile than the delay profile. Further subtype analyses suggested that social-affect symptoms were associated with greater hypoconnectivity than repetitive behavior symptoms in both clusters. Spatial correlation analyses with neurotransmitter maps revealed associations of Cluster 1 with mGluR5 and of Cluster 2 with GABAA α5, providing insight into the neurobiological basis of the two clusters. In a cross-disorder validation analysis, applying the same analytic framework to attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder did not reveal comparable results. Together, these findings suggest that ASD-related functional connectivity alterations are developmentally heterogeneous and organized along the cortical hierarchy, providing a developmental perspective for understanding the neurobiology of ASD.

item.title: Predicting individual differences in social functioning from functional connectomes in children with autism spectrum disorder.
item.description:
Psychiatry research
Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is characterized by profound heterogeneity in social functioning. While previous studies using group-level comparisons and predefined regions of interest have identified neural correlates of social deficits in ASD, the neural basis of individual differences in social functioning remains unclear. Here, we applied connectome-based predictive modeling to resting-state functional MRI data from 65 children with ASD aged 1.5-8 years (mean age = 4.23 years) to predict individual differences in social functioning assessed by the personal-social subscale of the Griffiths Development Scales (GDS). Results showed that whole-brain functional connectivity significantly predicted personal-social scores. The positive predictive network was dominated by connections within the default mode network, with the left precuneus emerging as a core hub. In contrast, the negative predictive network mainly involved inter-network connections, particularly between the frontoparietal and sensorimotor networks. In an independent cohort of 27 children with ASD aged 1.25-8 years (mean age = 3.31 years), the positive-edge model showed a significant association with personal-social scores, whereas the negative-edge and combined models did not. These findings suggest that intrinsic large-scale brain network organization is associated with individual differences in social functioning in children with ASD, highlighting the potential of network-level approaches for characterizing neurodevelopmental heterogeneity and supporting future precision-oriented research.

item.title: Cross-cohort transfer of clinical Alzheimer's EEG signatures to cognitively healthy APOE-ε4 and PICALM rs3851179 risk carriers using differentiable logic gate networks.
item.description:
Computers in biology and medicine
Neural alterations associated with Alzheimer's disease (AD) may emerge years before clinical diagnosis, and genetic risk factors such as APOE-ε4 and PICALM rs3851179 may identify individuals vulnerable to these shifts. We tested whether electroencephalography (EEG) signatures learned from clinically diagnosed AD patients transfer to cognitively healthy middle-aged adults carrying these variants. Differentiable logic gate networks (Diff-Logic) and neural baselines were trained on log-relative power spectral density features from a clinical cohort of AD patients and cognitively normal (CN) controls. These models were then applied without retraining to an independent genetic-risk cohort of neutral-risk non-carriers (N), APOE-ε4-only carriers (A+P-), and dual APOE-ε4/PICALM G-allele carriers (A+P+), yielding a continuous AD-like EEG signature score per participant. Diff-Logic matched neural baselines in clinical classification (balanced accuracy 0.809±0.028; AUROC 0.845±0.023) while enabling edge inference with a 7.4× model-size reduction and 0.22 ms model-only latency on a 7 W single-core CPU. In the genetic-risk cohort, scores were highest in A+P+ participants (0.393±0.167) relative to N (0.296±0.154) and A+P- (0.285±0.143; subject-level mean ± SD). This elevation was nominally significant before correction (A+P+ vs. A+P-, punc =0.036) but did not survive Holm correction (pHolm =0.109), and the cohort carried no AD pathology or conversion ground truth; the association was therefore exploratory. Integrated gradients attribution of the trained model showed genetic-risk relevance in delta, theta, and alpha, partially overlapping clinical AD topography. These findings support the feasibility of zero-shot EEG transfer in genetically at-risk individuals and highlight the need for replication in larger cohorts. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/Shyamal-Dharia/ad-difflogic-transfer.

item.title: Impact of sedation on the reliability of magnetoencephalographic language mapping in pediatric epilepsy.
item.description:
Epilepsia
Objective Magnetoencephalography (MEG) language mapping in pediatric epilepsy frequently requires sedation, which may alter cortical physiology and compromise the reliability of language lateralization. We hypothesized that sedation disrupts coupling between early auditory processing and higher order language networks, reducing the interpretability of laterality metrics. Methods Sixty-nine pediatric patients undergoing presurgical MEG evaluation were analyzed, including 32 nonsedated and 37 sedated participants. Auditory evoked field responses were quantified using the M200/M100 amplitude ratio and interhemispheric asymmetry. Language laterality indices (LIs) were derived from a continuous recognition memory paradigm, and source localization was performed using Fast-VESTAL. Results Sedation preferentially suppressed late auditory responses, reflected by a significant reduction in the M200/M100 ratio (p < .001) and increased interindividual variability. Despite preserved early sensory responses, auditory-language coupling was numerically attenuated under sedation. Notably, low M200/M100 ratios were frequently associated with highly lateralized LI values, suggesting reduced physiological reliability and the potential for "false certainty" in language lateralization. Source imaging demonstrated preserved primary auditory cortical activity with reduced recruitment of higher order association networks in sedated participants. Significance Sedation compromises the physiological reliability of MEG language lateralization by disrupting late auditory and association-level processing. The M200/M100 ratio provides a practical physiological marker for identifying cases in which laterality results should be interpreted with caution. These findings support a physiology-informed framework for improving the clinical interpretation of MEG language mapping in sedated pediatric patients, with direct implications for presurgical planning in pediatric epilepsy.

item.title: Human Hippocampal Theta-Gamma Phase-Amplitude Coupling Signals the Distance to Remembered Goals
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
In mammals, flexible navigation is believed to rely on a cognitive map of known locations supported by the hippocampus and surrounding medial temporal lobe structures. Hippocampal place cells typically exhibit spatial firing fields within a given environment. Moreover, their firing is modulated by the movement-related theta rhythm such that ‘theta sweeps’ of place cell activity encode the trajectory towards a hidden reward location during goal-directed navigation. Here, we attempted to detect signatures of theta sweeps in the human hippocampal local field potential (LFP) recorded with intracranial EEG. Specifically, we hypothesised that sequences of locations along a planned trajectory encoded by distinct cell assemblies are associated with gamma activity at successive theta phases. To test this hypothesis, we asked N=9 patients with epilepsy to perform a spatial navigation task in desktop virtual reality while we recorded LFP signals from depth electrode contacts implanted across the medial temporal lobe. Consistent with our predictions, we found an increase in hippocampal theta-gamma phase-amplitude coupling, a decrease in gamma power, and theta phase precession of gamma activity as hidden goal locations were approached and the sequence of locations remaining to be traversed became shorter. This suggests that goal-directed hippocampal theta sweeps during navigation are reflected in LFP theta-gamma phase-amplitude coupling, and that these neural mechanisms of model-based planning are conserved across species.

item.title: Beyond Gray Matter: White Matter Functional Network Signatures of Major Depressive Disorder Track Symptom Severity
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Resting-state neuroimaging studies in major depressive disorder (MDD) have consistently identified abnormalities across large-scale gray matter (GM) networks, including the default mode, salience, and sensorimotor systems. Although prior work has primarily focused on GM, evidence suggests that white matter (WM) hemodynamic signals are meaningful and reliable, supporting an active role for WM in brain function. A key gap remains in understanding WM functional network connectivity (FNC) and spectral characteristics in MDD. We used resting-state fMRI scans from the MDD-DIRECT phase II study, comprising 1,944 participants across 13 sites, to examine WM FNC and spectral characteristics in individuals with MDD and healthy controls using a spatially constrained independent component analysis (ICA) framework. This hybrid framework leverages ICA’s ability to identify spatially robust, functionally meaningful brain networks guided by replicable spatial priors to examine WM (1) FNC differences and (2) spectral power alterations between MDD and healthy participants. MDD was characterized by reduced long-range integrative connectivity alongside increased localized and limbic–sensorimotor coupling within WM networks, highlighting a systems-level imbalance in neural communication that may underlie core cognitive, affective, and somatic symptoms of depression. We also observed reduced low-frequency spectral power within frontal and subcortical WM systems involved in cognitive control, emotional regulation, and decision-making. Notably, both functional and spectral alterations were associated with clinical measures of depression and anxiety, with opposing associations observed for frontal connectivity patterns. Studying WM function alongside GM may provide a more comprehensive understanding of functional pathology in depression.

item.title: The Application of Video‑Electroencephalographic Monitoring Combined with Multimodal Imaging in Surgical Management of Secondary Epilepsy in Children
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Objective To explore the clinical value of video‑electroencephalography (VEEG) coupled with multimodal imaging for pre‑surgical epileptogenic‑zone localization, surgical planning and prognostic evaluation in children with drug‑resistant epilepsy. Methods : A retrospective analysis was performed on 42 pediatric patients who underwent epilepsy surgery. Pre‑operative workup included brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), long‑term scalp VEEG, and PET‑CT for selected participants. For diagnostically challenging cases, stereoelectroencephalography (SEEG) depth electrodes or electrocorticography (ECoG) cortical electrodes were implanted to refine epileptogenic‑zone identification. Cortical electrical stimulation (CES) and somatosensory evoked potentials (SEP) were applied to map eloquent brain regions. Intra‑operative cortical electrophysiological monitoring guided lesion resection. Individualized surgical strategies were adopted according to lesion characteristics. Post‑operative follow‑up spanned 1‑4 years, and seizure outcomes were assessed using the modified Engel classification. Results : ① Pre‑operative brain MRI revealed heterogeneous epileptogenic etiologies, most frequently temporal‑lobe signal abnormalities (17 cases) and focal cortical developmental anomalies (12 cases). ② Long‑term VEEG allowed detailed recording of background electroencephalographic rhythms; sleep markedly elevated the yield of interictal epileptiform discharges. Interictal discharges were captured in 35 patients, and spontaneous clinical seizure discharges were successfully recorded in 15 patients. ③ Among 21 patients receiving PET‑CT, focal hypometabolism was observed within most lesion territories. ④ Combined long‑term VEEG with intracranial SEEG/ECoG electrodes precisely delineated discharge onset zones, while functional‑mapping techniques ensured operative safety. ⑤ Ten distinct individualized surgical protocols were implemented tailored to underlying pathology. Intra‑operative ECoG detected sharp‑wave activity in 35 patients, informing the extent of surgical resection. ⑥ Integrating MRI findings with post‑surgical histopathology clarified the etiological diagnosis for all patients. ⑦ After 1‑4 years of follow‑up, 33 patients attained Engel class I outcomes, indicating satisfactory overall seizure control. Note: Developmental anomalies encompass structural malformations and signal alterations, collectively termed cortical developmental abnormalities herein. Conclusions :Video‑electroencephalography combined with multimodal imaging including MRI and PET‑CT enables reasonably accurate (though not absolute) dual anatomical‑electrophysiological localization of epileptogenic zones. This multimodal framework provides robust evidence for individualized surgical planning and bears considerable clinical utility.

item.title: Profound Tacrolimus-Induced Catatonic Encephalopathy in a Kidney Transplant Recipient With Mitochondrial Myopathy: A Cautionary Case of Reversible Neurotoxicity.
item.description:
Transplantation proceedings
Introduction Maternally inherited diabetes and deafness (MIDD) is a multisystem mitochondrial disorder most commonly caused by the m.3243A>G pathogenic variant in the MT-TL1 gene. Kidney transplantation in affected individuals presents unique perioperative and immunosuppressive management challenges due to underlying metabolic, neurologic, cardiac, and neuromuscular vulnerability. Case report We report a 64-year-old woman with end-stage renal disease secondary to insulin-dependent diabetes and MIDD (m.3243A>G) who underwent unrelated living donor kidney transplantation. The immediate postoperative period was complicated by diabetic ketoacidosis with lactic acidosis, transient slow graft function, and profound encephalopathy with catatonic features. Neuroimaging showed no acute abnormalities, and electroencephalography demonstrated severe diffuse encephalopathy without epileptiform activity. Tacrolimus levels were supratherapeutic in the early postoperative period. Given concern for calcineurin inhibitor neurotoxicity superimposed on mitochondrial dysfunction, tacrolimus was discontinued, and immunosuppression was switched to cyclosporine. Neurologic status gradually improved, and kidney allograft function fully normalized. Discussion This case highlights the substantial perioperative metabolic and neurologic risks associated with kidney transplantation in patients with MIDD. Patients with compensated cardiac dysfunction and manageable neuromuscular impairment should not be excluded from transplantation solely on the basis of mitochondrial cytopathy.

item.title: Dorsolateral prefrontal TMS-evoked N100 as a neurophysiological correlate of symptom change in adolescent depression.
item.description:
Journal of psychiatric research
Background Major depressive disorder (MDD) is highly prevalent in adolescence. Up to 30% of patients insufficiently benefit from first-line treatments, underscoring the need for improved treatment strategies and better understanding of pathophysiology. In depression, an imbalance between cortical excitation and inhibition in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC), assessed by the TMS-evoked N100 potential, is suggested as one of several contributing neurobiological mechanisms. While elevated N100 amplitudes have been observed in depressed adults and adolescents, its association with symptom change remains insufficiently investigated. Methods In a randomized controlled trial, N = 54 adolescents (38 girls, 16 boys) with MDD received six weeks of whole body vibration training (exercising on a vibrating plate that triggers involuntary muscle contractions through a neurological reflex) or light stretching as add-on treatments to treatment as usual. TMS-EEG was applied before and after the intervention to assess N100 amplitudes over the left and right DLPFC. Depressive symptoms were measured using the Children's Depression Rating Scale-Revised. Changes in N100 amplitudes were analyzed using repeated measures ANOVA. Multiple regression analyses with intervention group as predictor examined associations between changes in N100 amplitudes and depressive symptoms, including sex as moderator and a subsequent girls-only analysis. Results Across both groups, N100 amplitudes significantly decreased from pre-to post-intervention. No differential effects between interventions were observed. Reductions in right-hemispheric N100 amplitudes were significantly associated with improvements in depressive symptoms. This association reached statistical significance in girls. Conclusions Our findings support the N100 as a candidate neurophysiological correlate of depressive symptom improvement.

item.title: Analysis choices can produce apparent rich-club differences: an Alzheimer's disease EEG case study.
item.description:
Journal of neuroscience methods
Background The weighted rich-club coefficient tests whether a network's most strongly connected nodes are preferentially interconnected. Its interpretation depends on two often-implicit choices: how the randomised comparison networks are constructed, and whether the hubs are re-identified in each comparison network or held fixed at those of the observed network. When hubs are defined by connection strength, these choices change what the coefficient tests. New method We examined how these choices affect inference using resting-state EEG from 20 people with Alzheimer's disease and 20 controls. Holding the data fixed, we compared four analysis pipelines, crossing two ways of building the comparison networks (global weight reshuffle or strength-conditioned null) with the two hub choices, and ran a calibration study using data constructed to contain no preferential hub coupling beyond nodal strength. Results An apparent eyes-open group difference in rich-club organisation appeared only under the pipeline combining a global weight reshuffle with re-identified hubs. Under the empirical resampling ensemble, that pipeline reported a group difference in 43% of pseudo-studies, always higher in the Alzheimer's disease group, while the other three stayed near the expected 5%. Comparison with existing methods Unlike global weight reshuffling, strength-conditioned nulls approximately preserve nodal strengths; fixing observed hubs also retains the identity of the core being tested. Conclusions The same data can support or dissolve an apparent rich-club difference depending on these choices. No single choice is universally correct, but reporting which were made, and why they fit the question being asked, is essential to interpreting the result.

item.title: Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder Recognition Using the fNIRS Dual-Attention Network.
item.description:
Journal of neuroscience methods
Background Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is a prevalent psychological disorder that can impair daily functioning and mental health. Current clinical assessment mainly relies on structured interviews and symptom scales, which may introduce subjectivity and inter-rater variability. Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) provides a noninvasive approach for measuring task-evoked hemodynamic responses and may offer objective physiological information for auxiliary PTSD recognition. New method This study proposes an end-to-end deep learning framework, the fNIRS Dual Attention Network (FDANet), for PTSD recognition. Ten PTSD patients and ten healthy controls (HC) were recruited, and prefrontal hemodynamic signals, including oxyhemoglobin (HbO), deoxyhemoglobin (HbR), and total hemoglobin (HbT), were recorded during fear and neutral facial-expression stimuli. The three hemodynamic signals were concatenated along the channel dimension to form the model input. FDANet combines Transformer-based temporal modeling, one-dimensional temporal-channel attention, and convolutional feature extraction to learn discriminative representations from multichannel fNIRS signals. Results The model was evaluated using subject-wise nested cross-validation with five outer folds. At the trial level, FDANet achieved an accuracy of 79.4%. At the subject level, FDANet achieved an accuracy of 95.0%. Comparison with existing methods Compared with the evaluated traditional machine-learning and deep-learning baseline methods, FDANet achieved higher classification accuracy at both trial and subject levels. Conclusions These findings indicate that task-evoked prefrontal fNIRS signals contain discriminative information for PTSD recognition. Given the portability and noninvasive measurement characteristics of fNIRS, FDANet may support the future development of objective auxiliary screening tools for PTSD, although further validation with larger and independent samples is required.
